verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} one{H259} messenger{H4397} descending{H3381} from the heavens{H8064}, and to him was the key{H4668} of the deep{H8415}, and in his hand{H3027} a great{H1419} chain{H8333}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תְּהוֹם (tehom, H8415 — 'the deep') — the Genesis 1:2 primordial deep, consistent with ch. 17:8. Greek ἀβύσσου ('abyss') is related but tehom specifically evokes the pre-creation chaos. The adversary is confined in the primordial deep — pushed back to the pre-creation state.

Uses שַׁלְשֶׁלֶת (shalshelet, H8333 — 'chain') — a Hebrew word that also names one of the rarest Torah cantillation marks, appearing only four times in the entire Torah. The word itself connotes linkage and connection.

verses.translation: And he took{H3947} the dragon{H8577}, which is the adversary{H7854}, and bound{H631} him a thousand{H505} years{H8141}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַתַּנִּין (hatannin, H8577 — 'the dragon/sea-monster') — the OT chaos-creature (Gen 1:21 — 'God created the great tanninim'; Isa 27:1 — 'YHWH will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent... and he will slay the tannin that is in the sea'; Isa 51:9 — 'Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the tannin?'; Ezek 29:3, 32:2 — Pharaoh called a tannin). Greek δράκοντα ('dragon') is a Greek mythological creature. The Hebrew tanin is embedded in OT chaos-mythology and creation theology.

Hebrew identifies the dragon with ONE name: הַשָּׂטָן (hasatan — 'THE adversary'). Greek gives FOUR identifiers: τὸν δράκοντα τὸν ὄφιν τὸν ἀρχαῖον ὅς ἐστι Διάβολος καὶ Σατανᾶς ('the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the Devil and Satan'). The Hebrew is more concise — just 'the adversary.' Greek adds 'the ancient serpent,' 'the Devil' — absent from Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: one identifier — 'the adversary.' Greek: four identifiers — 'dragon, ancient serpent, Devil, Satan.' Greek massively expands the identification.
Hebrew uses feminine pronoun שֶׁהִיא (shehi — 'which she is') for the tannin, treating it as feminine.
translation_notes: 'Dragon' for tannin — the OT sea-monster of chaos, not the European dragon.
textual_notes: Isaiah 27:1 — 'In that day YHWH with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon (תנין) that is in the sea.'

verses.translation: And he cast{H7993} him into the deep{H8415} and shut{H5462} him and sealed{H2856} from above, so that he could not lead astray{H5496} the peoples{H5971} until the thousand{H505} years{H8141} were completed{H3615}; and after{H310} that he shall be freed a short{H4592} time.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֻפַּשׁ (chupash — 'freed/released') — from the root related to חָפְשִׁי (chofshi — 'free'), the specific SLAVE-EMANCIPATION term in the Torah (Ex 21:2 — 'in the seventh year he shall go out free [חפשי]'; Deut 15:12-13,18; Jer 34:9-16). Greek λυθῆναι ('to be loosed') is generic. The Hebrew describes the adversary's release using JUBILEE/SABBATICAL liberation vocabulary — the same language used for freeing Hebrew slaves. A back-translator from Greek 'loosed' would use יותר (yutar — 'loosed'), not the Torah emancipation term.
Uses לְהַסִּית (lehasit — 'to lead astray/incite', H5496) — consistently the Deut 13:6 incitement-to-idolatry verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'freed' (chupash — slave emancipation). Greek: 'loosed' (λυθῆναι — generic releasing).
translation_notes: חֻפַּשׁ (chupash) — later Hebrew passive form from the root חפש. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Exodus 21:2 — 'When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free (חפשי).' The sabbatical-release vocabulary applied to the adversary's temporary freedom.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} thrones{H3678}, and they sat{H3427} upon them, and to them was given{H5414} to judge{H8199}: those who believe{H539} and testify{H5749} concerning Yeshua, and those who did not take{H3947} upon their foreheads{H4696} the mark of the beast{H2416}, and did not pray{H6419} to it or to its image{H6459}; and these are alive{H2416} and ruling{H4910} with Yeshua a thousand{H505} years{H8141}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פֶּסֶל (pesel, H6459 — 'image/idol/carved image') — the specific SECOND COMMANDMENT term (Ex 20:4 — 'You shall not make for yourself a carved image [pesel]'; Deut 4:16,23,25, 5:8, 27:15). Greek: τῇ εἰκόνι ('the image') — a generic term. The Hebrew identifies the beast's image with the Torah's prohibition of idols. A back-translator from Greek εἰκών would use צלם (tselem — 'image'), not the commandment-specific pesel.

Uses מוֹשְׁלִים (moshlim — 'ruling', from mashal H4910 — 'to rule/have dominion'). Greek: ἐβασίλευσαν ('they reigned'). Hebrew mashal emphasizes dominion/governance; Greek basileuo emphasizes royal reign.

Uses מִצְחֵיהֶם (mitscheihem — 'their foreheads', H4696) — the same forehead word connected to the priestly plate in Ex 28:38, as in ch. 17:5. The mark is placed on the forehead — where the priestly holiness plate should be.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'image' (pesel — Torah idol). Greek: 'image' (εἰκών — generic). Different connotation.
Hebrew: 'prayed to it' (מתפללים). Greek: 'worshipped its image' (προσκυνοῦντας). Prayer vs. worship.
Greek adds 'those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God' (τὰς ψυχὰς τῶν πεπελεκισμένων...) — a whole clause absent from Hebrew.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:9-10,22 — 'Thrones were placed and the Ancient of Days took his seat... the court sat in judgment and the books were opened... judgment was given for the holy ones.' The throne-judgment scene from Daniel.

verses.translation: But the other{H312} dead{H4191} did not rise{H6965} until the thousand{H505} years{H8141} were completed{H3615}, and this is the first{H7223} resurrection.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תְּקוּמָה (tequmah — 'resurrection/rising') — from the root קום (qum, H6965 — 'to rise/stand up'). This is the Hebrew resurrection concept: the dead STAND UP. Greek ἀνάστασις ('resurrection') is from ἀνά + στάσις ('standing up'). Both languages use the 'rising/standing' metaphor, but the Hebrew form tequmah is distinctly later Hebrew.
translation_notes: תְּקוּמָה (tequmah) — a post-biblical Hebrew form from קום. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Daniel 12:2 — 'And many of those who sleep in the dust of the ground shall awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame and everlasting contempt.' The two-stage resurrection concept.

verses.translation: Holy{H6918} is the one who has a portion{H2506} in the first{H7223} resurrection, for over them there is no power{H3581} from a second{H312} death{H4194}; rather they shall be priests{H3548} to YHWH{H3068} and his anointed one, and ruling{H4910} with him a thousand{H505} years{H8141}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: קָדוֹשׁ הוּא (qadosh hu — 'HOLY is he'). Greek: Μακάριος καὶ ἅγιος ('BLESSED AND holy'). Hebrew has ONE quality (holy); Greek has TWO (blessed and holy). Greek adds 'blessed.' A back-translator from Greek would include both terms.

Uses חֵלֶק (cheleq, H2506 — 'portion/allotment') — the OT inheritance/allotment term. When YHWH is Israel's 'portion' (Ps 16:5, 73:26, 119:57, 142:5; Lam 3:24), the word cheleq is used. The resurrection is an INHERITANCE.
Uses כֹּחַ (koach, H3581 — 'power/strength'). Greek: ἐξουσίαν ('authority'). Hebrew: death has no PHYSICAL POWER; Greek: death has no INSTITUTIONAL AUTHORITY.

CRITICAL: Uses כֹּהֲנִים לְיַהְוֶה וּמְשִׁיחוֹ (kohanim la-YHWH umeshicho — 'priests to YHWH AND HIS ANOINTED ONE'). Greek: ἱερεῖς τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ ('priests of God and of Christ'). Hebrew preserves YHWH + מְשִׁיחוֹ (meshicho — 'his anointed one,' with the 3rd person possessive suffix, indicating YHWH's anointed). Greek uses God + Christos. The Hebrew construction 'his anointed' (meshicho) is the form found in Psalm 2:2 (עַל יהוה וְעַל מְשִׁיחוֹ — 'against YHWH and against his anointed one') and 1 Samuel 2:10, 2:35, 24:6,10, 26:9,11,16,23. A back-translator from Greek would write 'priests of God and of Christ,' not use the Psalm 2 construct form.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'holy' (one quality). Greek: 'blessed and holy' (two qualities).
Hebrew: 'YHWH and his anointed one.' Greek: 'God and Christ.'
Hebrew: 'power' (koach). Greek: 'authority' (exousia).
translation_notes: 'His anointed one' for meshicho — preserving the Psalm 2 possessive construct rather than importing the Greek title 'Christ.'
textual_notes: Psalm 2:2 — 'The kings of the earth set themselves... against YHWH and against his anointed one (משיחו).' The exact form used here.
Exodus 19:6 — 'You shall be to me a kingdom of priests (ממלכת כהנים).' The priestly-kingdom concept.

verses.translation: And after{H310} a thousand{H505} years{H8141} the adversary{H7854} shall be redeemed{H1350} from his captivity{H7628}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses יִגָּאֵל (yigga'el — 'shall be redeemed/released', from ga'al H1350). This is the KINSMAN-REDEEMER verb — the most theologically loaded word in the Hebrew legal system. The go'el (kinsman-redeemer) purchases back a relative's land (Lev 25:25), redeems a relative from slavery (Lev 25:48-49), avenges blood (Num 35:19-27), and — supremely — YHWH is Israel's Go'el (Isa 41:14, 43:1,14, 44:6,22-24, 47:4, 48:17,20, 49:7,26, 54:5,8, 59:20, 60:16, 63:16; Jer 50:34; Job 19:25). Greek λυθήσεται ('shall be loosed') is entirely generic. NO back-translator would EVER choose the go'el/redemption verb to translate Greek 'loosed.' This is perhaps the most theologically charged one-way marker in chapter 20.

Uses מִשִּׁבְיוֹ (mishivyo — 'from his captivity', from shevi H7628) — the standard OT war-captivity term (Num 21:1, Deut 21:10, Judg 5:12, Ps 68:18, 126:1, Jer 30:10, Ezek 39:25). Greek: ἐκ τῆς φυλακῆς αὐτοῦ ('from his prison'). Hebrew: war captivity; Greek: prison confinement.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall be redeemed' (go'el/kinsman-redeemer verb). Greek: 'shall be loosed.' Incompatible vocabulary choices.
Hebrew: 'from his captivity' (war prisoner). Greek: 'from his prison' (criminal confinement).
translation_notes: 'Redeemed' for yigga'el — preserving the astonishing use of the kinsman-redeemer verb for the adversary's release. This may suggest that even the adversary's temporary freedom serves YHWH's redemptive purpose.
textual_notes: Job 19:25 — 'I know that my Redeemer (גואלי, go'ali) lives.' The go'el verb carries the entire weight of divine redemption in the OT.

verses.translation: And he shall go{H3212} to lead astray{H5496} the peoples{H5971} upon the four{H702} corners{H6438} of the earth{H776}, even Gog{H1463} and Magog{H4031}, to gather{H622} his army{H2428} to come{H935} to the war{H4421}; and their number{H4557} is like the sand{H2344} of the sea{H3220}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כְּחוֹל הַיָּם (kechol hayam — 'like the sand of the sea') — the standard OT innumerability simile (Gen 22:17 — 'I will multiply your seed like the sand of the sea'; Gen 32:12, 41:49, Josh 11:4, Judg 7:12, 1 Sam 13:5, 2 Sam 17:11, 1 Ki 4:20). Greek uses the same simile — both traditions share this image from Genesis.
Uses חֵילֹו (cheilo — 'his army/force', from chayil H2428) — the OT military-resource term, same as ch. 21:24.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'to gather them together for war' (συναγαγεῖν αὐτοὺς εἰς πόλεμον). Hebrew has 'to gather his army to come to the war' — the subject gathered differs.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 38:2-9 — the Gog and Magog prophecy. The Hebrew author draws directly from Ezekiel's eschatological battle scenario.

verses.translation: And they trampled upon the breadth{H7341} of the ground{H127}, and surrounded{H5437} the holy{H6918} encampments{H2428} and the beloved{H157} city{H5892}; and fire{H784} fell{H5307} from the heavens{H8064} and burned{H8313} them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָאֲדָמָה (ha-adamah, H127 — 'the ground') again, not erets. Consistent pattern through these chapters.

Uses הָעִיר הָאֲהוּבָה (ha'ir ha-ahuvah — 'the beloved city', from ahav H157 — 'to love'). This echoes Psalm 87:2 (אֹהֵב יהוה שַׁעֲרֵי צִיּוֹן — 'YHWH loves the gates of Zion') and the prophetic tradition of Jerusalem as God's beloved. Greek: τὴν πόλιν τὴν ἠγαπημένην. Both use 'beloved.'

Uses הַחֵילוֹת הַקְּדוֹשִׁים (hacheilot hakedoshim — 'the holy encampments'). Greek: τὴν παρεμβολὴν τῶν ἁγίων ('the camp of the saints'). Hebrew uses chayil (H2428) in the military camp sense, while Greek uses παρεμβολή.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the ground' (adamah). Greek: 'the earth' (γῆ).
Greek adds 'and fire came down from God out of heaven' (ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ). Hebrew has simply 'fire from heavens' — without 'from God.'
textual_notes: 2 Kings 1:10-12 — fire falls from heaven at Elijah's command. The fire-from-heaven motif. Also Genesis 19:24 — fire and sulfur on Sodom.

verses.translation: And the adversary{H7854} who led them astray{H5496} was cast{H7993} into the fire{H784} of the Sheol{H7585} where the beast{H2416} and the prophet{H5030} of the falsehood{H8267} were; and they shall be afflicted{H6031} day{H3117} and night{H3915} from everlasting{H5769} to everlasting{H5769}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בָּאֵשׁ שֶׁל הַשְּׁאוֹל ('into the fire of the Sheol'). Greek: εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρὸς καὶ θείου ('into the lake of fire and sulfur'). The MOST persistent one-way marker in Revelation: Hebrew ALWAYS has 'fire of Sheol' where Greek has 'lake of fire.' The Hebrew locates the fiery judgment WITHIN Sheol — the OT underworld that burns (Deut 32:22 — 'a fire is kindled in my anger, and it burns to the depths of Sheol'). The Greek 'lake of fire' is a different concept entirely.

Uses יִתְעַנּוּ (yit'annu — 'they shall be afflicted', from anah H6031) — the specific YOM KIPPUR verb. Leviticus 16:29,31 and 23:27,29,32 command Israel to 'afflict your souls' (תענו את נפשתיכם) on the Day of Atonement. Greek βασανισθήσονται ('shall be tormented') is torture language. Hebrew: Yom Kippur affliction; Greek: punitive torment. A back-translator from Greek 'tormented' would use יענשו (ye'anshu — 'punished') or ייסרו (yeyassru — 'chastised'), not the Day of Atonement verb.

Uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם (me'olam ve'ad olam — 'from everlasting to everlasting') — the standard OT eternal formula (Ps 90:2, 103:17, 106:48, 1 Chr 16:36, 29:10, Neh 9:5). Greek: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of ages'). Different eternal formulas — the Hebrew is OT-rooted; the Greek is Hellenistic.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'fire of Sheol.' Greek: 'lake of fire and sulfur.' The most persistent divergence in Revelation.
Hebrew: 'afflicted' (Yom Kippur verb). Greek: 'tormented' (punishment verb).
Hebrew: 'from everlasting to everlasting.' Greek: 'unto the ages of ages.'
translation_notes: 'Afflicted' for yit'annu preserves the Yom Kippur connection — the eternal affliction is framed in Day of Atonement language.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 32:22 — 'For a fire is kindled in my anger, and it burns to the depths of Sheol (עד שאול תחתית).' The fire-in-Sheol concept.
Leviticus 16:29 — 'You shall afflict your souls (תענו את נפשתיכם).' The Yom Kippur affliction verb.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} [...] one{H259} great{H1419} throne{H3678}, and it was white{H3836}; and the one who sits{H3427} upon it — from before his face{H6440} the heavens{H8064} and the ground{H127} fled{H5127}, and no place{H4725} was found{H4672} for it.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נָס (nas — 'fled', from nus H5127 — 'to flee in terror'). This verb is used for fleeing from God's presence (Ex 14:27, Ps 68:1-2 — 'Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered; let those who hate him FLEE [ינוסו] before him'; Ps 104:7 — 'at your rebuke the waters FLED'). The heavens and ground flee in terror from the divine presence. Greek ἔφυγεν ('fled') is similar but nus carries the specific OT terror-flight connotation.
Again uses הָאֲדָמָה (ha-adamah — 'the ground', H127), not erets. Consistent.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the ground' (adamah). Greek: 'the earth' (γῆ).
Hebrew has a lacuna [...] in the text.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:9 — 'Thrones were placed and the Ancient of Days took his seat; his clothing was white as snow.' The white throne scene from Daniel.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} the dead{H4191}, both the small{H6996} and the great{H1419}, standing{H5975} before{H6440} YHWH{H3068}; and the scrolls{H5612} were opened{H6605}, and another{H312} scroll{H5612} was opened{H6605}, and this is the scroll{H5612} of life{H2416}; to judge{H8199} the dead{H4191} according to what is written{H3789} in the scrolls{H5612} and according to their deeds{H4639}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לִפְנֵי יַהְוֶה (lifnei YHWH — 'before YHWH', H3068). Greek: ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ ('before God'). The dead stand before the covenant-name God, not merely before 'God.'

Uses סֵפֶר הַחַיִּים (sefer hachayyim — 'the scroll of life') — the OT concept (Ex 32:32-33 — Moses says 'if not, blot me from your scroll [ספרך] which you have written'; Ps 69:28 — 'let them be blotted from the book of the living [ספר חיים]'; Dan 12:1 — 'everyone found written in the book [ספר]'). Greek: τὸ βιβλίον τῆς ζωῆς. Both preserve the concept.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'before YHWH.' Greek: 'before God.' (Some Greek manuscripts have 'before the throne.')
Greek adds 'according to their works' (κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν) at the end. Hebrew also has 'according to their deeds' (כפי מעשיהם).
textual_notes: Daniel 7:10 — 'The court sat in judgment and the books (ספרין) were opened.' The opened-books judgment scene from Daniel.

verses.translation: And the sea{H3220} emptied out{H7324} the dead{H4191} that were in it, and the death{H4194} and the Sheol{H7585} gave{H5414} up the dead{H4191}; and each{H259} one was judged{H8199} according to his deeds{H4639}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses וַיָּרֶק (vayyareq — 'and emptied out', from riq H7324 — 'to empty/pour out'). This verb is used for emptying containers (Gen 42:35 — 'as they emptied their sacks'; Jer 48:12 — 'who shall empty [ירקו] his vessels'). The sea DISGORGES its dead as one empties a container. Greek ἔδωκεν ('gave up') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use נתנה (natnah — 'gave'), not the vivid emptying/pouring verb.
Uses הַשְּׁאוֹל (hash'ol — 'the Sheol', H7585). Greek: ὁ ᾅδης ('Hades'). Hebrew Sheol and Greek Hades are related underworld concepts but carry different theological traditions.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'emptied out' (vivid pouring verb). Greek: 'gave up' (generic).

verses.translation: And the death{H4194} and the Gehinnom were cast{H7993} into the fire{H784}, and this is a second{H312} death{H4194}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַגֵּיהִנֹּם (haGeihinnom — 'the Gehinnom/Gehenna') — the Valley of (the Son of) Hinnom, the specific GEOGRAPHICAL LOCATION south of Jerusalem where child sacrifice to Molech was performed (2 Ki 23:10, Jer 7:31-32, 19:2-6, 32:35, 2 Chr 28:3, 33:6). Greek: ὁ ᾅδης ('Hades' — the Greek underworld). The Hebrew author DISTINGUISHES between Sheol (used in v13 for the generic underworld) and Gehinnom (used here for the place of judgment). Greek uses Hades for BOTH, losing this critical distinction. A back-translator from Greek Hades would use Sheol consistently, not switch to Gehinnom. The Sheol/Gehinnom distinction is native to Hebrew/Jewish theological discourse — Sheol is where all dead go; Gehinnom is the place of judgment. This distinction exists ONLY in Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'cast into the fire' (באש). Greek: 'cast into the lake of fire' (εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρός). Hebrew has simply 'fire'; Greek has 'lake of fire.' The Hebrew never uses the 'lake' concept.

Greek adds: 'this is the second death, the lake of fire' (Οὗτος ὁ θάνατος ὁ δεύτερός ἐστιν, ἡ λίμνη τοῦ πυρός) — an identification clause equating the second death WITH the lake of fire. Hebrew simply says 'this is a second death' — without the lake-of-fire identification.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Gehinnom' (valley of Hinnom — geographical). Greek: 'Hades' (Greek underworld — mythological). MOST significant divergence.
Hebrew: 'fire.' Greek: 'lake of fire.'
Greek adds interpretive identification: 'the second death IS the lake of fire.'
translation_notes: 'Gehinnom' is preserved untranslated — it is a specific geographical name (Valley of Hinnom) that became the Jewish term for the place of post-mortem judgment.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 7:31-32 — 'They have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (גיא בן הנם), to burn their sons and daughters in the fire... therefore behold, days are coming when it shall no longer be called Topheth or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter.' The geographical origin of Gehinnom as a place of judgment.

The Sheol/Gehinnom distinction: In v13, the Hebrew uses שאול (Sheol — the generic underworld where all dead reside). In v14, it switches to גיהנם (Gehinnom — the specific place of fiery judgment). This two-tier afterlife geography is standard in Jewish thought (see Mishnah, Avot 5:22; Tosefta, Sanhedrin 13:3) but does not exist in Greek thought, which has only Hades.

verses.translation: And if one{H259} was not found{H4672} written{H3789} in the scroll{H5612} of life{H2416}, he was cast{H7993} into the fire{H784}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: 'cast into the fire' (באש). Greek: 'cast into the lake of fire' (εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρός). Hebrew has 'fire'; Greek has 'lake of fire.' Consistent to the end.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'fire.' Greek: 'lake of fire.'
textual_notes: Psalm 69:28 — 'Let them be blotted out of the book of the living (ספר חיים), and not be enrolled among the righteous.' The inverse of being found in the scroll of life.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 20 in Hebrew contains several of the most theologically significant one-way markers in the entire book. The most striking are: (1) The SHEOL/GEHINNOM DISTINCTION (v13 uses שאול/Sheol for the generic underworld; v14 switches to גיהנם/Gehinnom for the place of judgment) — a two-tier afterlife geography that exists in Hebrew/Jewish thought but is absent from Greek, which uses Hades for both; (2) The GO'EL VERB (יגאל, v7) for the adversary's release — using the kinsman-redeemer vocabulary rather than generic 'loosing'; (3) The CHUPASH (חפש, v3) slave-emancipation term for the adversary's temporary freedom — Sabbatical/Jubilee release language; (4) The YOM KIPPUR AFFLICTION VERB (יתענו, v10) for eternal punishment — framing eschatological judgment in Day of Atonement language; (5) 'Fire of Sheol' (v10) vs. Greek 'lake of fire' — the persistent pattern; (6) PESEL (פסל, v4) — the Second Commandment idol term; (7) כהנים ליהוה ומשיחו ('priests to YHWH and his anointed one') using the Psalm 2:2 construct form; (8) מעולם ועד עולם ('from everlasting to everlasting') — the OT eternal formula vs. Greek 'ages of ages'; and (9) TANNIN (תנין, v2) — the OT chaos-monster vs. Greek 'dragon.' The chapter demonstrates a Hebrew author thinking in Jewish theological categories (Sheol vs. Gehinnom, go'el redemption, Yom Kippur affliction, Torah idolatry concepts) that are systematically flattened in the Greek translation.
